transcript:
Meeting: WaveFront - Concurrency Surge & Streaming Backpressure Playthrough
Date: 2026-03-30 11:00am PDT
Duration: 68 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Jonas (Redwood SE), Aisha (WF Head of Platform), Devon (WF Infra), Liam (WF PM)

Summary: quick demo showing long-context sessions under bursty TPS, how streaming behaves when backend queues fill, and what fallbacks look like across Dedicated/Hosted.

[00:00] Maya Patel: Hey everyone thanks for joining, quick intros?
[00:08] Aisha Rahman: Hi, Aisha here. We run the real-time personalization platform, want to understand how Redwood handles our peak windows.
[00:14] Devon Cruz: Devon, infra. We're worried about 10-15k TPS spikes and long conversation histories up to 200k tokens, plus streaming for partial responses.
[00:22] Jonas Kim: Great context. We'll demo three things: sustained high TPS with long context, streaming backpressure when token generation is slower, and timeouts/TTL behavior plus model variant fallback.
[00:33] Liam O'Neill: Quick Q up front: are you expecting us to use Dedicated or Hosted for pilot?
[00:37] Maya Patel: We'll show both. Dedicated for predictable throughput; hosted with routing policies for cost-tiered fallbacks.

[05:12] Jonas Kim: (screen share) Console -> Routes. Here's policy: route by region, then prefer Dedicated pool A for this tenant. If Dedicated saturates, fallback to hosted low-cost model with a "shorter context".
[05:28] Devon Cruz: When you say "shorter context" what gets truncated? We keep last 50k tokens of KV cache, is that possible?
[05:34] Jonas Kim: Practically we keep the active KV prefix; but for fallback we can set a history truncation policy — e.g., reduce to last 8k tokens. That gets tuned per workload.

[12:05] (Demo: synthetic traffic generator) Jonas Kim: Starting surge now. We're simulating 12k TPS for 10 minutes with a mixture of long-history sessions and quick hits. Streaming enabled.
[12:19] (Noise - typing)
[12:31] Speaker 1: Uh hm, saw the initial drop, streaming chunk arrives at 300ms normally...
[12:45] Aisha Rahman: We're seeing chunk delays on our side too. How is Redwood batching interacting with streaming?
[12:52] Jonas Kim: Good callout. Continuous batching groups tokens across sessions up to latency SLO. When queue grows, batching windows widen slightly which can increase first-byte latency; but overall token throughput increases.
[13:20] Jonas Kim: Also K-V cash — sorry K-V cache — helps avoid recomputing prefixes so long sessions don't re-run full context, but if cache eviction happens under memory pressure, you'll see step changes in latency.

[20:40] (Surge increases)
[20:49] Devon Cruz: We're watching the Console: Dedicated pool shows backpressure flags. What exactly triggers fallback to hosted?
[20:57] Maya Patel: Policy-based thresholds. On this template we set 85% GPU util or queue depth > X to start canarying 10% traffic to hosted variants. If latency exceeds SLO for N seconds, escalation opens.
[21:14] Liam O'Neill: Does canarying maintain session stickiness? We can't split a single long session across models.
[21:22] Jonas Kim: Right, sessions are sticky by default. When we canary, new sessions are routed; existing long sessions stay on the original pool until they end or TTL expires. You can opt into forced session migration but that's risky for KV coherence.

[28:01] (Simulated streaming slowdown)
[28:10] Jonas Kim: Now slowing token generation to simulate a heavy decode kernel. You'll see partials arrive slower and at some point we hit streaming timeouts configured in the route.
[28:29] (System message) Speaker 2: [inaudible] timeout...
[28:33] Aisha Rahman: So when a streaming client times out, what happens on the server side? We need guarantees about token completion or at least idempotent resumes.
[28:42] Jonas Kim: If client closes connection, the runtime keeps the work for a configurable grace period (we call it stream-ttl). If the client reconnects with the same session token within TTL, it can pick up from last committed KV state. If TTL expires, KV eviction may happen.
[28:58] Devon Cruz: That sounds good, but what's the default TTL?
[29:03] Jonas Kim: Default is 60s for streaming TTL, configurable per-route up to minutes depending on retention and memory budget.

[34:10] Liam O'Neill: If the fallback model uses a shorter context, do you re-run the prompt prefix to refill KV? That sounds expensive.
[34:19] Jonas Kim: We try to avoid re-running full prefix. Instead we synthesize a condensed context — an extractive summary — then resume. That reduces re-run cost but may degrade quality; we flag that in the Console.

[40:05] (Latency spike shown)
[40:12] Maya Patel: Demoing automatic truncation: when queue depth crosses threshold we trim oldest messages beyond the route's history window and offload them to cheap object storage for audit. This is visible in logs.
[40:30] Devon Cruz: For compliance we need full raw history for 90 days. Can Redwood keep raw transcripts even after truncation?
[40:40] Jonas Kim: Yes, audit logs and full transcript storage are separate. You can configure retention to keep raw inputs in your S3/GCS/KMS-encrypted bucket. We only trim in-memory KV for runtime efficiency.

[50:20] (Edge case: many long sessions plus sudden QoS drop)
[50:28] Jonas Kim: Now simulating a network partition in one region; routing will failover to another region which triggers model variant fallback because different regions have different capacity.
[50:41] Aisha Rahman: Do customers see a visible model change? Concerned about hallucination differences across model sizes.
[50:48] Jonas Kim: We tag responses with model version and a quality confidence score. Console surfaces regression alerts when the quality delta exceeds a threshold for a monitored prompt set.

[59:00] (Questions)
[59:07] Devon Cruz: On the Dedicated pool, what knobs reduce GPU memory during high concurrency?
[59:12] Jonas Kim: Several: offload KV to NVM, enable lower-precision quantization, or limit per-session context to a sliding window. Also batching optimizations and kernel selection reduce memory pressure.

[62:55] Liam O'Neill: For our pilot we want to try 2 weeks on Dedicated, start with 2 gpus equivalent for baseline then ramp. Can you provide expected unit cost numbers for that traffic profile?
[63:05] Maya Patel: We'll send a cost estimate based on your sample traffic. Jonas will run the trial and capture token-level breakdowns.

[66:10] (Wrap) Maya Patel: Quick recap: Maya to share benchmark sheet + pricing, Jonas to stand up Dedicated trial and run customer prompts, Devon to share network/VPC details. We'll reconvene after initial trial run.
[66:30] Aisha Rahman: Thanks everyone, this was concrete and helpful.
[66:37] Maya Patel: Thanks all.

Notes on transcript quality: several words mis-transcribed (K-V cash, canarying spelled as 'canarying' in audio), occasional overlapping talk, timestamps approximated.
